{{Short description|Graph of an equation}}
[[File:Superellipse chamfered square.svg|thumb|Lamé's special quartic with "radius" 1.]]
'''Lamé's special quartic''', named after [[Gabriel Lamé]], is the [[Graph  of a function|graph]] of the [[equation]]

:<math>x^4 + y^4 = r^4</math>

where <math>r > 0</math>.<ref>{{citation|title=Analytic Geometry Problems|volume=108|series=College Outline Series|first=Cletus Odia|last=Oakley|publisher=Barnes & Noble|year=1958|page=171}}.</ref>  It looks like a rounded [[Square (geometry)|square]] with "sides" of length <math>2r</math> and centered on the origin.  This curve is a [[squircle]] centered on the origin, and it is a special case of a [[superellipse]].<ref>{{citation|title=The Words of Mathematics: An Etymological Dictionary of Mathematical Terms Used in English|series=MAA Spectrum|first=Steven|last=Schwartzman|publisher=Mathematical Association of America|year=1994|isbn=9780883855119|page=212|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SRw4PevE4zUC&pg=PA212}}.</ref>

Because of [[Pierre de Fermat]]'s only surviving [[mathematical proof|proof]], that of [[Proof of Fermat's Last Theorem for specific exponents#n=4|the ''n'' = 4 case]] of [[Fermat's Last Theorem]], if ''r'' is [[Rational number|rational]] there is no non-trivial rational point (''x'', ''y'') on this curve (that is, no point for which both ''x'' and ''y'' are non-zero rational numbers).
